that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A **sequence in $X$** is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$, written $(x_k)$ with
$x_k := x(k)$. As everywhere in this library, $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]) and a sequence is indexed from $0$
([[def-sequence]]); an index range copied from a text that starts at $1$ must be
shifted before it is used here.

Let $(x_k)$ be a sequence in $X$ and $p \in X$. The function
$k \mapsto d(x_k, p)$ is a sequence of reals ([[def-sequence]]), and it is
nonnegative ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]), so $|d(x_k,p)| = d(x_k,p)$
([[def-abs-value]]). Define

$$x_k \longrightarrow p \text{ in } (X,d) \quad :\Longleftrightarrow \quad d(x_k,p) \longrightarrow 0 \text{ in } \mathbb{R},$$

the convergence on the right being that of [[def-real-limit]]. Unwound, this
says: for every **rational** $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$d(x_k, p) < \varepsilon$ for every $k \ge K$. We then call $p$ a **limit** of
$(x_k)$, and say $(x_k)$ **converges** in $(X,d)$ if it has a limit.

**Rational and real $\varepsilon$ agree here, as they do on the real line.**
[[def-real-limit]] tests convergence against rational $\varepsilon$ only, and its
own remark, restated for sequences in [[def-sequence]], records that nothing is
lost: below any real $\eta > 0$ lies a positive rational
([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), and the index belonging to that rational serves for
$\eta$. So a proof may establish convergence by producing an index for every
real $\varepsilon > 0$, and may use a convergence hypothesis at a real
$\varepsilon$ by first passing to a rational below it. Both moves are used on
this page and are always cited.

**Subsequences and subsequential limits.** A **subsequence** of $(x_k)$ is the
composite $x \circ n$ for a strictly increasing $n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$,
written $(x_{n_j})$, exactly as for sequences of reals ([[def-sequence]]); and
$p$ is a **subsequential limit** of $(x_k)$ in $(X,d)$ when some subsequence
converges to $p$, which is the metric-space form of [[def-subsequential-limit]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and open covers, subcovers, finiteness and compactness as
in [[def-metric-compactness]].

- $(X,d)$ is **countably compact** when every open cover $\mathcal{U}$ of $X$
  that is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) has a finite subcover.
- $(X,d)$ is **sequentially compact** when every sequence $(x_k)$ in $X$, that is
  every function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-sequence]]), has a subsequence
  $(x_{n_j})$ converging to a point of $X$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]), the
  index map $n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ being strictly increasing
  ([[lem-index-map-grows]]).
- $(X,d)$ is **limit point compact** when every infinite subset $A \subseteq X$
  has a limit point in $X$, that is a point $p \in X$ with
  $B(p,r) \cap (A \setminus \{p\}) \ne \emptyset$ for every real $r > 0$
  ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]). Here *infinite* means not finite in
  the sense of [[def-countable]], equivalently not listable as
  $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ and not empty ([[def-metric-compactness]]).

A subset $A \subseteq X$ is called countably compact, sequentially compact or
limit point compact when the metric subspace $(A, d_A)$ is
([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]), exactly as for compactness.

**The countable covers may be listed.** A nonempty at most countable family
$\mathcal{U}$ admits a surjection $\mathbb{N} \to \mathcal{U}$
([[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]]), so countable compactness says: for
every sequence $(U_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of open sets with
$X = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} U_n$ there are finitely many indices whose sets
already cover $X$. That surjection is produced from the countability assumption
alone and no choice principle is involved; the empty family covers only the empty
space, which is compact anyway.

**Limit points are computed where the set lives.** For $S \subseteq A \subseteq X$
and $a \in A$, the identity $B_A(a,r) = B_X(a,r) \cap A$
([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]) shows that $a$ is a limit point of $S$ in
the subspace $(A,d_A)$ exactly when $a$ is a limit point of $S$ in $X$ and lies in
$A$. So "$A$ is limit point compact" says that every infinite $S \subseteq A$ has
a limit point **belonging to $A$**; a limit point outside $A$ does not count, and
that is what distinguishes the property from a statement about $X$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $A \subseteq X$, let
$x \in X$ and let $F \subseteq X$. Call $F$ **sequentially closed** when every
sequence in $F$ that converges in $X$ has its limit in $F$. Then:

1. $x \in \overline{A}$ ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]) if and only if
   there is a sequence $(a_k)$ with $a_k \in A$ for every $k$ and $a_k \to x$ in
   $(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]).
2. $F$ is closed ([[def-metric-topology]]) if and only if $F$ is sequentially
   closed.

**The Axiom of Countable Choice is used, once.** The direction of claim 1 that
manufactures a sequence out of adherence makes one choice per natural number, and
that is exactly $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). The converse
direction, and the direction of claim 2 that goes from closed to sequentially
closed, are choice free. This is flagged at the step that spends it.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $(x_k)$ be a
sequence in $X$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]). If $x_k \to p$ and $x_k \to q$,
then $p = q$.

So a convergent sequence in a metric space has exactly one limit, and the
notation $\lim_k x_k$ is unambiguous.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A **sequence in $X$** is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$, written $(x_k)$ with
$x_k := x(k)$. As everywhere in this library, $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]) and a sequence is indexed from $0$
([[def-sequence]]); an index range copied from a text that starts at $1$ must be
shifted before it is used here.

Let $(x_k)$ be a sequence in $X$ and $p \in X$. The function
$k \mapsto d(x_k, p)$ is a sequence of reals ([[def-sequence]]), and it is
nonnegative ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]), so $|d(x_k,p)| = d(x_k,p)$
([[def-abs-value]]). Define

$$x_k \longrightarrow p \text{ in } (X,d) \quad :\Longleftrightarrow \quad d(x_k,p) \longrightarrow 0 \text{ in } \mathbb{R},$$

the convergence on the right being that of [[def-real-limit]]. Unwound, this
says: for every **rational** $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$d(x_k, p) < \varepsilon$ for every $k \ge K$. We then call $p$ a **limit** of
$(x_k)$, and say $(x_k)$ **converges** in $(X,d)$ if it has a limit.

**Rational and real $\varepsilon$ agree here, as they do on the real line.**
[[def-real-limit]] tests convergence against rational $\varepsilon$ only, and its
own remark, restated for sequences in [[def-sequence]], records that nothing is
lost: below any real $\eta > 0$ lies a positive rational
([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), and the index belonging to that rational serves for
$\eta$. So a proof may establish convergence by producing an index for every
real $\varepsilon > 0$, and may use a convergence hypothesis at a real
$\varepsilon$ by first passing to a rational below it. Both moves are used on
this page and are always cited.

**Subsequences and subsequential limits.** A **subsequence** of $(x_k)$ is the
composite $x \circ n$ for a strictly increasing $n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$,
written $(x_{n_j})$, exactly as for sequences of reals ([[def-sequence]]); and
$p$ is a **subsequential limit** of $(x_k)$ in $(X,d)$ when some subsequence
converges to $p$, which is the metric-space form of [[def-subsequential-limit]].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]].

- An **open cover** of $(X,d)$ is a family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$
  with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$, where
  $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily
  $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \emptyset$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,d)$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite subcover: for
  every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \emptyset$ and the empty subfamily
  covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the metric
  subspace $(A, d_A)$ is a compact metric space, $d_A$ being the restriction of
  $d$ to $A \times A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A,d_A)$ and its own open sets, not
about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do agree,
but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], and no item of this library may use the
ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading as the
definition is what makes "compact" a property of the metric space $(A,d_A)$
alone, so that a set compact in one ambient space is compact in every other one
containing it isometrically.

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. The
one-point space is compact too, and so is every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$: given a cover, each $x_i$ lies in some member, and
finitely many members chosen in this way already cover.

**The finiteness convention, and how it is used both ways.** "Finite" above is
the listing form, matching the finite lists of
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. It agrees with the definition of
finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number ([[def-countable]]), and
both directions of the agreement are available and are used below:

- A nonempty finite set $F$ in the sense of [[def-countable]] satisfies
  $F \approx m$ for some $m \ge 1$, and a bijection $m \to F$ is exactly a
  listing $F = \{a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}\}$.
- Conversely a set listed as $A = \{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$, that is the image of a
  function $a$ with domain $\sigma(n)$, is finite in the sense of
  [[def-countable]]: the map sending $x \in A$ to the least $i \le n$ with
  $a_i = x$ is an injection of $A$ into $\sigma(n)$, so $A$ is equinumerous with
  a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ bounded above, and such a subset is finite
  ([[lem-subset-of-countable]]).

Neither direction uses a choice principle: the second selects nothing, taking a
least index instead.

derivations.claim: Shift invariance of the code: fix $s\in X_\pm$ and define $y_n:=x_{n+1}(s)$ for $n\in\mathbb Z$. Then, using $T_{S_\pm s}$ and [F1], $$\bigl(T_{S_\pm s}y\bigr)_n=(S_\pm s)_n\sqrt{a+y_{n-1}+y_{n+1}}=s_{n+1}\sqrt{a+x_n(s)+x_{n+2}(s)}=\bigl(T_sx(s)\bigr)_{n+1}=x_{n+1}(s)=y_n ;$$ thus $y$ is a fixed point of $T_{S_\pm s}$ in $B_R$, and by the uniqueness clause of [F1] (via [[lem-coded-quadratic-recurrence-is-a-contraction]]) $y=x(S_\pm s)$, i.e. $x_n(S_\pm s)=x_{n+1}(s)$ for all $n$.
$F|_\Lambda$ is continuous: $F$ has polynomial components, hence is continuous on $\mathbb R^2$, and a restriction of a continuous map is continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]).

Conjugacy identity: for $s\in X_\pm$, [F1] and step 1.1 give $F(h(s))=F(x_{-1}(s),x_0(s))=(x_0(s),x_1(s))=(x_{-1}(S_\pm s),x_0(S_\pm s))=h(S_\pm s)$. Hence $F(h(X_\pm))\subseteq h(X_\pm)$, and since $S_\pm$ is onto, for every $h(s)\in h(X_\pm)$ the identity applied to $S_\pm^{-1}s$ gives $h(s)=F(h(S_\pm^{-1}s))\in F(h(X_\pm))$; therefore $F(\Lambda)=\Lambda$.

$h$ is a homeomorphism: $h$ is a continuous bijection of $X_\pm$ onto $\Lambda$ by [F1]. To prove that $h^{-1}$ is continuous it suffices to prove that $h$ maps closed subsets of $X_\pm$ to closed subsets of $\mathbb R^2$. Let $C\subseteq X_\pm$ be closed. Then $C$ is sequentially compact: a sequence in $C$ has a subsequence converging in the sequentially compact space $X_\pm$ ([F2] and the isometry $\varphi$ of [F1]), and the limit lies in $C$ because $C$ is closed and therefore sequentially closed by the choice-free direction of [F4]. The continuous image $h(C)$ is sequentially compact: given a sequence $(h(x_k))$ with $x_k\in C$, pick a subsequence $x_{k_j}$ converging to some $x\in C$, then $h(x_{k_j})\to h(x)\in h(C)$ by continuity ([[def-metric-compactness-variants]], [[def-metric-continuity]]); no choice is used beyond the single subsequence selection that sequential compactness of $C$ provides. Moreover $h(C)$ is sequentially closed: if a sequence in $h(C)$ converges, then some subsequence converges to a point of $h(C)$ by the previous paragraph (with that sequence in place of the given one), and the whole sequence has the same limit by uniqueness of limits ([F4]); hence the limit lies in $h(C)$. By the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ direction of [F4] the sequentially closed set $h(C)$ is closed in $\mathbb R^2$. Thus $h$ is a closed map, so $h^{-1}$ is continuous and $h$ is a homeomorphism.

Sensitivity: let $z=h(s)\in\Lambda$ and $\varepsilon>0$; choose $m\ge0$ with $4\sqrt2\,RL^{-m}<\varepsilon$ and let $k\ge m+1$. Define $t\in X_\pm$ by $t_k:=-s_k$ and $t_j:=s_j$ for $j\ne k$. Then $s,t$ agree for all $|j|\le m$, so by the coding-continuity clause of [F1] ([[lem-symbol-locality-gives-coding-continuity]]) one has $\|h(s)-h(t)\|_2\le4\sqrt2\,RL^{-m}<\varepsilon$. On the other hand $S_\pm^k s$ and $S_\pm^k t$ differ exactly at coordinate $0$, so their signs at $0$ are opposite; by [F1], $\bigl|x_0(S_\pm^k s)-x_0(S_\pm^k t)\bigr|\ge|x_0(S_\pm^k s)|+|x_0(S_\pm^k t)|\ge2L$. Using step 2.1, $F^k(z)=F^k(h(s))=h(S_\pm^ks)$ and $F^k(h(t))=h(S_\pm^kt)$, so $\bigl\|F^k(z)-F^k(h(t))\bigr\|_2\ge\bigl|x_0(S_\pm^ks)-x_0(S_\pm^kt)\bigr|\ge2L$. Thus $2L$ is a sensitivity constant.

$\Lambda$ is sequentially compact: $X_2$ is sequentially compact without choice ([F2]); since $\varphi:X_\pm\to X_2$ is a bijective isometry ([F1]), a sequence in $X_\pm$ is carried to a sequence in $X_2$ with a convergent subsequence whose preimage under $\varphi$ converges in $X_\pm$ to the corresponding preimage limit; hence $X_\pm$ is sequentially compact. Applying the continuous-image argument of step 3.1 with $C=X_\pm$ shows that $\Lambda=h(X_\pm)$ is sequentially compact.

$\Lambda$ is compact under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega+\mathrm{DC}$ [F5]: $X_2$ is compact by [F2]; since $\varphi$ is a bijective isometry, a set $U\subseteq X_\pm$ is open exactly when $\varphi(U)\subseteq X_2$ is open, so the images under $\varphi$ of an open cover of $X_\pm$ form an open cover of $X_2$, whose finite subcover pulls back to a finite subcover of the original cover; hence $X_\pm$ is compact. A continuous image of a compact space is compact by [[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]], so $\Lambda=h(X_\pm)$ is compact.

Topological mixing of $F|_\Lambda$: let $U,V\subseteq\Lambda$ be nonempty and open in $\Lambda$; then $h^{-1}(U)$ and $h^{-1}(V)$ are nonempty open subsets of $X_\pm$ (step 3.1). Since $S_\pm$ is topologically mixing ([F2], transferred through the isometry $\varphi$ of [F1] and the conjugacy $S_\pm=\varphi^{-1}\circ\sigma_2\circ\varphi$), there is $N$ with $S_\pm^n\bigl(h^{-1}(U)\bigr)\cap h^{-1}(V)\ne\emptyset$ for every $n\ge N$; applying $h$ and step 2.1, $F^n(U)\cap V=h\Bigl(S_\pm^n\bigl(h^{-1}(U)\bigr)\cap h^{-1}(V)\Bigr)\ne\emptyset$ for every $n\ge N$.

Dense periodic points: a point $s$ is periodic for $S_\pm$ if and only if $h(s)$ is periodic for $F|_\Lambda$, by the conjugacy of step 2.1 and the injectivity of $h$ ([F1]). Since $h$ is a bijection carrying the topology of $X_\pm$ onto that of $\Lambda$ (steps 2.1, 3.1 and [[def-dense-top]]), it maps the dense set of periodic points of $S_\pm$ ([F2]) to a dense subset of $\Lambda$ consisting of periodic points of $F|_\Lambda$.

Conclusion: by steps 1.2, 4.3, 4.4 and 3.2, the restriction $F|_\Lambda$ is continuous, topologically mixing, has dense periodic points and is sensitive with constant $2L$; by the definition of [[def-cm-topologically-mixing-dense-periodic-and-sensitive-maps]] it is chaotic in the stated sense, and clauses 1-4 are proved.

boundaries.reason: The invariant set Lambda is the image of the nonempty shift space and is nonempty by construction; the statement makes no claim about an empty invariant set.

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.1 shows Lambda is sequentially compact and the statement's uses the strictly positive sensitivity constant 2L; the fixed points h(bar u) are distinct points of Lambda computed in step 1.2 and the statement's.
Step 1.1 proves the shift identity for a single code s, and step 1.2 then upgrades it to all s by bijectivity of S_pm; both the one-step and all-times statements are checked.

Step 5.1 includes the periodic codes and the nonperiodic ones: the sensitivity proof of step 5.1 flips one distant symbol, and step 4.3 records that periodic points of S_pm correspond exactly to periodic points of F on Lambda.

boundaries.reason: The statement has no interval endpoints; the only limiting operations are the two-sided limits n->+-infinity, which are not part of this theorem but of the homoclinic-orbit lemma.

boundaries.evidence: the statement's states exactly where AC_omega is spent (the sequential-closure direction of [F4]) and step 4.1 records that compactness uses AC_omega+DC through the published compactness of X_2; no other step uses a choice principle.
Step 1.2 proves F(h(s))=h(S_pm s) and hence F(Lambda) subset Lambda, the forward invariance inclusion.
Step 1.2 also applies the identity to S_pm^{-1}s to obtain h(s) in F(Lambda), giving the reverse inclusion and the equality F(Lambda)=Lambda.

citations.quote:
Fix $a\ge100$ and put

$$R:=\sqrt a+3,\qquad L:=\sqrt{\,a-2R\,}.$$

Let $X_{\pm}$ and $B_R$ be the two-sign shift space and the closed ball of bounded bilateral sequences of [[def-bilateral-symbol-and-bounded-sequence-space]], and for $s\in X_{\pm}$ define

$$T_s:B_R\longrightarrow \mathbb R^{\mathbb Z},\qquad (T_sx)_n:=s_n\sqrt{\,a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}\,}\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z).$$

Then:

1. $a-2R=(\sqrt a-1)^2-7\ge74$, so $L\ge\sqrt{74}>1$; moreover $a+2R<R^2$, hence $\sqrt{a+2R}<R$;
2. for every $s\in X_{\pm}$ and $x\in B_R$ the radicands $a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}$ lie in $[a-2R,a+2R]\subseteq(0,\infty)$, so $T_sx$ is a well-defined bounded sequence with $\|T_sx\|_\infty\le\sqrt{a+2R}<R$; in particular $T_s(B_R)\subseteq B_R$;
3. for all $x,y\in B_R$ and every $s\in X_{\pm}$,

$$\|T_sx-T_sy\|_\infty\le\frac1L\,\|x-y\|_\infty,\qquad \frac1L<1 ;$$

4. hence $T_s$ has, for each $s\in X_{\pm}$, exactly one fixed point $x(s)\in B_R$, and for every $n\in\mathbb Z$

$$\operatorname{sign}x_n(s)=s_n,\qquad |x_n(s)|\ge L,\qquad x_{n+1}(s)+x_{n-1}(s)=x_n(s)^2-a .$$

Fix $a\ge100$ and let $R=\sqrt a+3$, $L=\sqrt{a-2R}$, $X_\pm$, $D_\pm$ and $B_R$ be as in [[def-bilateral-symbol-and-bounded-sequence-space]] and [[lem-coded-quadratic-recurrence-is-a-contraction]]. Define the **quadratic phase map**

$$F:\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad F(x,y):=(y,\;y^2-a-x),$$

and for each $s\in X_\pm$ let $x(s)$ be the unique fixed point of $T_s$ in $B_R$. Define the **coding map**

$$h:X_\pm\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad h(s):=\bigl(x_{-1}(s),\,x_0(s)\bigr).$$

Then:

1. $F$ is a bijection with $F^{-1}(x,y)=(x^2-a-y,\,x)$, and for every $s\in X_\pm$ and $n\in\mathbb Z$

$$F\bigl(x_{n-1}(s),x_n(s)\bigr)=\bigl(x_n(s),x_{n+1}(s)\bigr);$$

2. **(locality)** for all $m\ge0$, $n\in\mathbb Z$ and $s,t\in X_\pm$: if $s_j=t_j$ for all $j$ with $|j-n|\le m-1$, then $\bigl(T_s^m0\bigr)_n=\bigl(T_t^m0\bigr)_n$, where $T_s^m$ is the $m$-fold iterate and $0$ the zero sequence;
3. **(uniform error)** for all $m\ge0$ and $s\in X_\pm$,

$$\bigl\|T_s^m0-x(s)\bigr\|_\infty\le 2R\,L^{-m};$$

4. **(coding continuity)** if $s,t\in X_\pm$ agree at every coordinate $j$ with $|j|\le m$, then $|x_n(s)-x_n(t)|\le4R\,L^{-m}$ for $n\in\{-1,0\}$, and consequently

$$\bigl\|h(s)-h(t)\bigr\|_2\le4\sqrt2\,R\,L^{-m};$$

in particular $h$ is continuous at every $s\in X_\pm$ ([[def-metric-continuity]]) when $X_\pm$ carries $D_\pm$ and $\mathbb R^2$ the Euclidean metric;

5. **(injectivity)** $h$ is injective.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

**The quadratic family.** For $a\in\mathbb R$ let

$$F_a:\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad F_a(x,y):=(y,\,y^2-a-x),$$

with differential and inverse differential at $(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$

$$DF_a(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&2y\end{pmatrix},\qquad DF_a(x,y)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2x&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix};$$

the matrices act on column vectors of $\mathbb R^2$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). The inverse differential is displayed as the differential of $F_a^{-1}(x,y)=(x^2-a-y,x)$.

**Cones.** Fix $k\in(0,1)$. The **unstable cone** and **stable cone** of aperture $k$ are

$$C^u_k:=\{\,(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2\ :\ |u|\le k|v|\,\},\qquad C^s_k:=\{\,(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2\ :\ |v|\le k|u|\,\}$$

([[def-abs-value]]); both are closed subsets of $\mathbb R^2$, they are closed under multiplication by real scalars, and $C^u_k\cap C^s_k=\{0\}$, because a nonzero vector in the intersection would satisfy $|u|\le k|v|$ and $|v|\le k|u|$, hence $|u|\le k^2|u|<|u|$.

**Slopes.** A line through the origin not contained in the vertical axis is written uniquely as $\{(hv,v):v\in\mathbb R\}$ with the **slope parameter** $h=u/v$; here $|h|\le k$ characterises the lines contained in $C^u_k$. Similarly a line not contained in the horizontal axis is written uniquely as $\{(u,ru):u\in\mathbb R\}$ with the **slope parameter** $r=v/u$, and $|r|\le k$ characterises the lines contained in $C^s_k$.

For real numbers $x,y$ two maps on slope parameters are defined:

$$\Phi_y(h):=\frac{1}{2y-h}\quad(h\ne2y)\quad\text{(forward slope map)},\qquad \Psi_x(r):=\frac{1}{2x-r}\quad(r\ne2x)\quad\text{(backward slope map)}.$$

The intended reading is the graph-transform reading: $DF_a(x,y)$ carries the line $\{(hv,v)\}$ at $(x,y)$ to the line $\{(h'v,v)\}$ at $F_a(x,y)$ with $h'=\Phi_y(h)$, and $DF_a(x,y)^{-1}$ carries the line $\{(u,ru)\}$ at $(x,y)$ to the line $\{(u,r'u)\}$ at $F_a^{-1}(x,y)$ with $r'=\Psi_x(r)$. These two statements are assertions about the displayed matrices and are proved in the companion lemma on this page, not part of this definition.

**Invariant line fields on a sequence.** Let $s=(s_n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real bilateral sequence and let $z_n:=(s_{n-1},s_n)$. An **unstable line field along $s$** is a family $(L^u_n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ of lines through the origin of $\mathbb R^2$ such that $DF_a(z_n)$ maps $L^u_n$ onto $L^u_{n+1}$ for every $n$; a **stable line field along $s$** is a family $(L^s_n)$ with $DF_a(z_n)^{-1}$ mapping $L^s_{n+1}$ onto $L^s_n$ for every $n$. Existence and uniqueness of line fields with slopes in $[-k,k]$ for sequences with $|s_n|\ge L$ are proved in the companion lemma on this page.

**Stable and unstable sets, homoclinic and transverse homoclinic points.** Let $G:Z\to Z$ be a bijection of a metric space $(Z,d)$ ([[def-metric-space]]) with fixed point $\bar z$ (so $G(\bar z)=\bar z$). Put

$$W^s(\bar z):=\{\,z\in Z\ :\ G^n(z)\ \text{is defined for every }n\ge0\text{ and }G^n(z)\to\bar z\ \text{as }n\to\infty\,\},$$

$$W^u(\bar z):=\{\,z\in Z\ :\ G^{-n}(z)\ \text{is defined for every }n\ge0\text{ and }G^{-n}(z)\to\bar z\ \text{as }n\to\infty\,\},$$

where convergence is that of the metric $d$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]). The sets $W^s(\bar z)$ and $W^u(\bar z)$ are the **stable set** and the **unstable set** of $\bar z$. A **homoclinic point** of $\bar z$ is a point $z\in W^s(\bar z)\cap W^u(\bar z)$ with $z\ne\bar z$.

A homoclinic point $z$ is **transverse** when there are $\varepsilon>0$ and $C^1$ maps ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-derivative]])

$$\gamma_s,\gamma_u:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\longrightarrow Z$$

such that $\gamma_s(0)=\gamma_u(0)=z$, $\gamma_s\bigl((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\bigr)\subseteq W^s(\bar z)$, $\gamma_u\bigl((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\bigr)\subseteq W^u(\bar z)$, both $\gamma_s$ and $\gamma_u$ are injective on $(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ with $\gamma_s'(0)\ne0\ne\gamma_u'(0)$, and the tangent vectors $\gamma_s'(0)$ and $\gamma_u'(0)$ are linearly independent. The interval $(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ is that of [[def-interval]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A **sequence in $X$** is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$, written $(x_k)$ with
$x_k := x(k)$. As everywhere in this library, $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]) and a sequence is indexed from $0$
([[def-sequence]]); an index range copied from a text that starts at $1$ must be
shifted before it is used here.

Let $(x_k)$ be a sequence in $X$ and $p \in X$. The function
$k \mapsto d(x_k, p)$ is a sequence of reals ([[def-sequence]]), and it is
nonnegative ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]), so $|d(x_k,p)| = d(x_k,p)$
([[def-abs-value]]). Define

$$x_k \longrightarrow p \text{ in } (X,d) \quad :\Longleftrightarrow \quad d(x_k,p) \longrightarrow 0 \text{ in } \mathbb{R},$$

the convergence on the right being that of [[def-real-limit]]. Unwound, this
says: for every **rational** $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$d(x_k, p) < \varepsilon$ for every $k \ge K$. We then call $p$ a **limit** of
$(x_k)$, and say $(x_k)$ **converges** in $(X,d)$ if it has a limit.

**Rational and real $\varepsilon$ agree here, as they do on the real line.**
[[def-real-limit]] tests convergence against rational $\varepsilon$ only, and its
own remark, restated for sequences in [[def-sequence]], records that nothing is
lost: below any real $\eta > 0$ lies a positive rational
([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), and the index belonging to that rational serves for
$\eta$. So a proof may establish convergence by producing an index for every
real $\varepsilon > 0$, and may use a convergence hypothesis at a real
$\varepsilon$ by first passing to a rational below it. Both moves are used on
this page and are always cited.

**Subsequences and subsequential limits.** A **subsequence** of $(x_k)$ is the
composite $x \circ n$ for a strictly increasing $n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$,
written $(x_{n_j})$, exactly as for sequences of reals ([[def-sequence]]); and
$p$ is a **subsequential limit** of $(x_k)$ in $(X,d)$ when some subsequence
converges to $p$, which is the metric-space form of [[def-subsequential-limit]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$
