citations.quote:
**The normalized pulse.** Fix once and for all a function

$$w\in C_c^\infty\bigl((0,1)\bigr),\qquad w\ge0,\qquad \int_0^1w(s)\,ds=1 .$$

Such a function exists: by [[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]] there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty((0,1))$ with $\chi\ge0$ and $\chi(1/2)>0$, and $w:=\chi/\int_0^1\chi$ has the stated properties, the integral being positive. All constructions below use only these properties of $w$ and are therefore independent of the particular choice.

**The periodic pulse.** Fix a real parameter $a\ge100$ and a smallness parameter $\delta>0$, and put $P:=\pi/2+\delta$. Define $\beta_\delta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ to be the $P$-periodic function whose restriction to $[0,P]$ is

$$\beta_\delta(t):=0\quad\Bigl(t\in\Bigl[0,\tfrac\pi2\Bigr]\Bigr),\qquad \beta_\delta(t):=\frac1\delta\,w\Bigl(\frac{t-\pi/2}{\delta}\Bigr)\quad\Bigl(t\in\Bigl[\tfrac\pi2,P\Bigr]\Bigr).$$

Both definitions are meaningful: for $t\in[\pi/2,P]$ the argument $(t-\pi/2)/\delta$ lies in $[0,1]$, and at the junction $t=\pi/2$ the second formula gives $\delta^{-1}w(0)=0$ because $w$ is supported in the open interval $(0,1)$; at $t=P$ it gives $\delta^{-1}w(1)=0$. Every derivative of $w$ vanishes at $0$ and $1$ (as $w$ is $C^\infty$ and compactly supported in $(0,1)$), so the $P$-periodic extension is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Moreover

$$\beta_\delta\ge0,\qquad \int_0^P\beta_\delta(t)\,dt=\int_0^1w(s)\,ds=1 .$$

**The Hamiltonian and its equations.** On canonical coordinates $(q,p)\in\mathbb R^2$ define

$$H_\delta:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad H_\delta(t,q,p):=\frac{p^2+q^2}{2}+\beta_\delta(t)\Bigl(aq-\frac{q^3}{3}\Bigr).$$

The associated first-order system is

$$q'=p,\qquad p'=-q+\beta_\delta(t)\,(q^2-a),$$

equivalently the second-order equation $q''=-q+\beta_\delta(t)(q^2-a)$; the right-hand side is $C^\infty$ in $(t,q,p)$, hence continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, so every initial condition has a unique maximal solution ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], [[def-maximal-ode-solution]], [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]). The system is $P$-periodic in $t$.

**Free rotation and pulse endpoint maps.** Over the first subinterval $[0,\pi/2]$ the pulse vanishes and the system is the free oscillator; define the **free rotation**

$$R_0:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2,\qquad R_0(q,p):=(p,-q),$$

which is the time-$\pi/2$ solution operator of $q'=p$, $p'=-q$: the map $t\mapsto(q_0\cos t+p_0\sin t,\,-q_0\sin t+p_0\cos t)$ solves the free system with the initial data $(q_0,p_0)$, and uniqueness of solutions identifies it with the solution operator.

For $s\in[0,1]$ the **rescaled pulse equation** is

$$q_s=\delta\,p,\qquad p_s=-\delta\,q+w(s)\,(q^2-a),$$

obtained from the second half of the period by the substitution $s=(t-\pi/2)/\delta$. For $(q,p)$ in its domain of existence, let the **pulse endpoint map** be

$$K_\delta(q,p):=\bigl(q(1),p(1)\bigr),$$

where $s\mapsto(q(s),p(s))$ is the unique solution of the rescaled equation with $(q,p)(0)=(q,p)$ ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]). The **stroboscopic map** of the periodic system,

$$G_\delta:=K_\delta\circ R_0,$$

is defined on the set of $(q,p)\in\mathbb R^2$ for which the solution of the $P$-periodic system exists up to time $P$; there it equals the stroboscopic map $\theta_P$ of [[def-cm-stroboscopic-map]]: the free rotation moves the initial point to time $\pi/2$, and the pulse endpoint map moves it from time $\pi/2$ to time $P$.

Fix $a\ge100$, put $R:=\sqrt a+3\ge13$, $S:=[-R-1,R+1]^2$, and let $w$, $\delta$, $P$, $\beta_\delta$, $R_0$, the rescaled pulse equation, the endpoint map $K_\delta$ and the stroboscopic map $G_\delta=K_\delta\circ R_0$ be as in [[def-smooth-periodic-oscillator-pulse-model]]. Let

$$K(q,p):=(q,\,p+q^2-a),\qquad F(q,p):=(p,\,p^2-a-q),\qquad J:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},$$

so that $F=K\circ R_0$. Then there are constants $\delta_1>0$ and $C_1<\infty$ depending only on $a$ and $w$ such that for every $0<\delta\le\delta_1$:

1. **(existence on the pulse)** for every $(q,p)\in S$ the solution of the rescaled equation with initial data $(q,p)$ exists on $[0,1]$ and stays in the compact tube $T:=[-R-2,R+2]\times[-M,M]$, $M:=R+1+(R+1)^2+1$; hence $K_\delta$ is defined on $S$, $K_\delta(S)\subseteq T$, and

$$\sup_{S}\bigl(|K_\delta-K|+\|DK_\delta-DK\|\bigr)\le C_1\delta$$

for the Euclidean norm and the operator norm;
2. **(closeness of the period map)** $\sup_S\bigl(|G_\delta-F|+\|DG_\delta-DF\|\bigr)\le C_1\delta$;
3. **(smoothness, invertibility, symplecticity)** $G_\delta$ is of class $C^\infty$ on an open neighbourhood $N$ of $S$; $DG_\delta(z)$ is invertible for every $z\in N$ and $G_\delta$ is injective on $N$, so $G_\delta:N\to G_\delta(N)$ is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism onto its image; and

$$DG_\delta(z)^{\mathsf T}J\,DG_\delta(z)=J\qquad(z\in N),$$

that is, $G_\delta$ is symplectic;
4. **(the reverse-conjugated map)** let $S_w(q,p):=(p,q)$ and $H_\delta:=S_w\circ G_\delta^{-1}\circ S_w$ on a neighbourhood of $S$. Then $H_\delta$ is of class $C^\infty$ there, and there is $C_2<\infty$, depending only on $a$ and $w$, with

$$\sup_{S}\bigl(|H_\delta-F|+\|DH_\delta-DF\|\bigr)\le C_2\delta .$$

Consequently, for every $\delta$ small enough that $\varepsilon:=\max(C_1,C_2)\delta$ satisfies $\varepsilon\le1/6$ and $C\varepsilon\le1$ ($C$ the constant of the perturbed-recurrence lemma on this page), the maps $G_\delta$ and $H_\delta$ satisfy all hypotheses of the perturbed horseshoe theorem on this page on the square $S$.

Fix $a\ge100$ and put

$$R:=\sqrt a+3,\qquad l:=\sqrt a-3\ge7,\qquad S:=[-R-1,R+1]^2,\qquad S(x,y):=(y,x).$$

Let $C=C(a,R)$ be the constant of [[lem-perturbed-scalar-recurrence-root-bounds]], let $0<\varepsilon\le1/6$ with $\eta:=C\varepsilon\le1$, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open with $S\subseteq U$. Let $G=(A,B):U\to\mathbb R^2$ be a $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto its image whose components satisfy, on $S$,

$$|A(x,y)-y|\le\varepsilon,\quad |\partial_xA(x,y)|\le\varepsilon,\quad |\partial_yA(x,y)-1|\le\varepsilon,$$

$$|B(x,y)-(y^2-a-x)|\le\varepsilon,\quad |\partial_xB(x,y)+1|\le\varepsilon,\quad |\partial_yB(x,y)-2y|\le\varepsilon,$$

and assume in addition that $H:=S\circ G^{-1}\circ S$ is defined and of class $C^2$ on a neighbourhood of $S$ and satisfies the same six inequalities on $S$ with the same constant $\varepsilon$. For each sign $u$ let $M_u$ be the root map of [[lem-perturbed-scalar-recurrence-root-bounds]] applied to $G$, let $V$ be the inverse branch of [[lem-close-map-first-component-has-uniform-inverse]], and let $M^H_u,V^H$ be the corresponding objects for $H$. Then:

1. **(coding)** for every $s\in X_\pm$ there is exactly one $q(s)\in B_R$ with $q_n(s)=M_{s_n}\bigl(q_{n-1}(s),q_{n+1}(s)\bigr)$ for all $n\in\mathbb Z$; it satisfies $l\le|q_n(s)|\le R$, $\operatorname{sign}q_n(s)=s_n$ and $R-|q_n(s)|\ge\tfrac34$, $|q_n(s)|-l\ge\tfrac34$; setting $v_n(s):=V(q_n(s),q_{n+1}(s))$ and

$$z_n(s):=\bigl(q_n(s),v_n(s)\bigr),\qquad h_G(s):=z_0(s)=\bigl(q_0(s),V(q_0(s),q_1(s))\bigr),$$

one has $G(z_n(s))=z_{n+1}(s)$ for all $n$;
2. **(conjugacy and chaos)** $h_G$ is a continuous bijection of $(X_\pm,D_\pm)$ onto $\Lambda_G:=h_G(X_\pm)$; granting the Axiom of Countable Choice (used once, through the equivalence between closed and sequentially closed subsets of $\mathbb R^2$), it is a homeomorphism, and $G\circ h_G=h_G\circ S_\pm$, so $\Lambda_G$ is $G$-invariant; $\Lambda_G$ is sequentially compact, and compact under the Axioms of Countable and Dependent Choice; and $G|_{\Lambda_G}$ is continuous, topologically mixing, has dense periodic points, and is sensitive with sensitivity constant $2l$; hence $G|_{\Lambda_G}$ is chaotic in the stated sense;
3. **(fixed points)** for each sign $u$ the constant code $\bar u$ gives a fixed point $z_{\bar u}:=h_G(\bar u)=\bigl(\rho_u,V(\rho_u,\rho_u)\bigr)$, where $\rho_u=M_u(\rho_u,\rho_u)$ is the unique element of $u\,[l,R]$ with $\rho_u=M_u(\rho_u,\rho_u)$; these two fixed points are hyperbolic;
4. **(transverse homoclinic points)** let $s\in X_\pm$ be nonconstant with $s_n=u$ for $|n|\ge N$. Then $z_*:=h_G(s)\ne z_{\bar u}$, and there are $C^1$ curves $\gamma_s,\gamma_u:(-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)\to\mathbb R^2$ with $\gamma_s(0)=\gamma_u(0)=z_*$, $\gamma_s\bigl((-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)\bigr)\subseteq W^s(z_{\bar u})$, $\gamma_u\bigl((-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)\bigr)\subseteq W^u(z_{\bar u})$, tangent vectors $\gamma_s'(0)\in C^s_{3/4}$, $\gamma_u'(0)\in C^u_{3/4}$; since $C^s_{3/4}\cap C^u_{3/4}=\{0\}$ the tangent lines are distinct, so $z_*$ is a transverse homoclinic point of $z_{\bar u}$ ([[def-stable-unstable-cones-and-line-slopes]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Fix $a\ge100$ and put

$$R:=\sqrt a+3,\qquad l:=\sqrt a-3\ge7,\qquad S:=[-R-1,R+1]^2,\qquad S(x,y):=(y,x).$$

Let $C=C(a,R)$ be the constant of [[lem-perturbed-scalar-recurrence-root-bounds]], let $0<\varepsilon\le1/6$ with $\eta:=C\varepsilon\le1$, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open with $S\subseteq U$. Let $G=(A,B):U\to\mathbb R^2$ be a $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto its image whose components satisfy, on $S$,

$$|A(x,y)-y|\le\varepsilon,\quad |\partial_xA(x,y)|\le\varepsilon,\quad |\partial_yA(x,y)-1|\le\varepsilon,$$

$$|B(x,y)-(y^2-a-x)|\le\varepsilon,\quad |\partial_xB(x,y)+1|\le\varepsilon,\quad |\partial_yB(x,y)-2y|\le\varepsilon,$$

and assume in addition that $H:=S\circ G^{-1}\circ S$ is defined and of class $C^2$ on a neighbourhood of $S$ and satisfies the same six inequalities on $S$ with the same constant $\varepsilon$. For each sign $u$ let $M_u$ be the root map of [[lem-perturbed-scalar-recurrence-root-bounds]] applied to $G$, let $V$ be the inverse branch of [[lem-close-map-first-component-has-uniform-inverse]], and let $M^H_u,V^H$ be the corresponding objects for $H$. Then:

1. **(coding)** for every $s\in X_\pm$ there is exactly one $q(s)\in B_R$ with $q_n(s)=M_{s_n}\bigl(q_{n-1}(s),q_{n+1}(s)\bigr)$ for all $n\in\mathbb Z$; it satisfies $l\le|q_n(s)|\le R$, $\operatorname{sign}q_n(s)=s_n$ and $R-|q_n(s)|\ge\tfrac34$, $|q_n(s)|-l\ge\tfrac34$; setting $v_n(s):=V(q_n(s),q_{n+1}(s))$ and

$$z_n(s):=\bigl(q_n(s),v_n(s)\bigr),\qquad h_G(s):=z_0(s)=\bigl(q_0(s),V(q_0(s),q_1(s))\bigr),$$

one has $G(z_n(s))=z_{n+1}(s)$ for all $n$;
2. **(conjugacy and chaos)** $h_G$ is a continuous bijection of $(X_\pm,D_\pm)$ onto $\Lambda_G:=h_G(X_\pm)$; granting the Axiom of Countable Choice (used once, through the equivalence between closed and sequentially closed subsets of $\mathbb R^2$), it is a homeomorphism, and $G\circ h_G=h_G\circ S_\pm$, so $\Lambda_G$ is $G$-invariant; $\Lambda_G$ is sequentially compact, and compact under the Axioms of Countable and Dependent Choice; and $G|_{\Lambda_G}$ is continuous, topologically mixing, has dense periodic points, and is sensitive with sensitivity constant $2l$; hence $G|_{\Lambda_G}$ is chaotic in the stated sense;
3. **(fixed points)** for each sign $u$ the constant code $\bar u$ gives a fixed point $z_{\bar u}:=h_G(\bar u)=\bigl(\rho_u,V(\rho_u,\rho_u)\bigr)$, where $\rho_u=M_u(\rho_u,\rho_u)$ is the unique element of $u\,[l,R]$ with $\rho_u=M_u(\rho_u,\rho_u)$; these two fixed points are hyperbolic;
4. **(transverse homoclinic points)** let $s\in X_\pm$ be nonconstant with $s_n=u$ for $|n|\ge N$. Then $z_*:=h_G(s)\ne z_{\bar u}$, and there are $C^1$ curves $\gamma_s,\gamma_u:(-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)\to\mathbb R^2$ with $\gamma_s(0)=\gamma_u(0)=z_*$, $\gamma_s\bigl((-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)\bigr)\subseteq W^s(z_{\bar u})$, $\gamma_u\bigl((-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)\bigr)\subseteq W^u(z_{\bar u})$, tangent vectors $\gamma_s'(0)\in C^s_{3/4}$, $\gamma_u'(0)\in C^u_{3/4}$; since $C^s_{3/4}\cap C^u_{3/4}=\{0\}$ the tangent lines are distinct, so $z_*$ is a transverse homoclinic point of $z_{\bar u}$ ([[def-stable-unstable-cones-and-line-slopes]]).

**The quadratic family.** For $a\in\mathbb R$ let

$$F_a:\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad F_a(x,y):=(y,\,y^2-a-x),$$

with differential and inverse differential at $(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$

$$DF_a(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&2y\end{pmatrix},\qquad DF_a(x,y)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2x&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix};$$

the matrices act on column vectors of $\mathbb R^2$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). The inverse differential is displayed as the differential of $F_a^{-1}(x,y)=(x^2-a-y,x)$.

**Cones.** Fix $k\in(0,1)$. The **unstable cone** and **stable cone** of aperture $k$ are

$$C^u_k:=\{\,(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2\ :\ |u|\le k|v|\,\},\qquad C^s_k:=\{\,(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2\ :\ |v|\le k|u|\,\}$$

([[def-abs-value]]); both are closed subsets of $\mathbb R^2$, they are closed under multiplication by real scalars, and $C^u_k\cap C^s_k=\{0\}$, because a nonzero vector in the intersection would satisfy $|u|\le k|v|$ and $|v|\le k|u|$, hence $|u|\le k^2|u|<|u|$.

**Slopes.** A line through the origin not contained in the vertical axis is written uniquely as $\{(hv,v):v\in\mathbb R\}$ with the **slope parameter** $h=u/v$; here $|h|\le k$ characterises the lines contained in $C^u_k$. Similarly a line not contained in the horizontal axis is written uniquely as $\{(u,ru):u\in\mathbb R\}$ with the **slope parameter** $r=v/u$, and $|r|\le k$ characterises the lines contained in $C^s_k$.

For real numbers $x,y$ two maps on slope parameters are defined:

$$\Phi_y(h):=\frac{1}{2y-h}\quad(h\ne2y)\quad\text{(forward slope map)},\qquad \Psi_x(r):=\frac{1}{2x-r}\quad(r\ne2x)\quad\text{(backward slope map)}.$$

The intended reading is the graph-transform reading: $DF_a(x,y)$ carries the line $\{(hv,v)\}$ at $(x,y)$ to the line $\{(h'v,v)\}$ at $F_a(x,y)$ with $h'=\Phi_y(h)$, and $DF_a(x,y)^{-1}$ carries the line $\{(u,ru)\}$ at $(x,y)$ to the line $\{(u,r'u)\}$ at $F_a^{-1}(x,y)$ with $r'=\Psi_x(r)$. These two statements are assertions about the displayed matrices and are proved in the companion lemma on this page, not part of this definition.

**Invariant line fields on a sequence.** Let $s=(s_n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real bilateral sequence and let $z_n:=(s_{n-1},s_n)$. An **unstable line field along $s$** is a family $(L^u_n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ of lines through the origin of $\mathbb R^2$ such that $DF_a(z_n)$ maps $L^u_n$ onto $L^u_{n+1}$ for every $n$; a **stable line field along $s$** is a family $(L^s_n)$ with $DF_a(z_n)^{-1}$ mapping $L^s_{n+1}$ onto $L^s_n$ for every $n$. Existence and uniqueness of line fields with slopes in $[-k,k]$ for sequences with $|s_n|\ge L$ are proved in the companion lemma on this page.

**Stable and unstable sets, homoclinic and transverse homoclinic points.** Let $G:Z\to Z$ be a bijection of a metric space $(Z,d)$ ([[def-metric-space]]) with fixed point $\bar z$ (so $G(\bar z)=\bar z$). Put

$$W^s(\bar z):=\{\,z\in Z\ :\ G^n(z)\ \text{is defined for every }n\ge0\text{ and }G^n(z)\to\bar z\ \text{as }n\to\infty\,\},$$

$$W^u(\bar z):=\{\,z\in Z\ :\ G^{-n}(z)\ \text{is defined for every }n\ge0\text{ and }G^{-n}(z)\to\bar z\ \text{as }n\to\infty\,\},$$

where convergence is that of the metric $d$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]). The sets $W^s(\bar z)$ and $W^u(\bar z)$ are the **stable set** and the **unstable set** of $\bar z$. A **homoclinic point** of $\bar z$ is a point $z\in W^s(\bar z)\cap W^u(\bar z)$ with $z\ne\bar z$.

A homoclinic point $z$ is **transverse** when there are $\varepsilon>0$ and $C^1$ maps ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-derivative]])

$$\gamma_s,\gamma_u:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\longrightarrow Z$$

such that $\gamma_s(0)=\gamma_u(0)=z$, $\gamma_s\bigl((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\bigr)\subseteq W^s(\bar z)$, $\gamma_u\bigl((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\bigr)\subseteq W^u(\bar z)$, both $\gamma_s$ and $\gamma_u$ are injective on $(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ with $\gamma_s'(0)\ne0\ne\gamma_u'(0)$, and the tangent vectors $\gamma_s'(0)$ and $\gamma_u'(0)$ are linearly independent. The interval $(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ is that of [[def-interval]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) with its metric topology ([[def-metric-topology]]) and let $f:X\to X$ be a map. For $n\ge1$ write $f^n$ for the $n$-fold iterate, $f^1:=f$ and $f^{n+1}:=f\circ f^n$.

1. $f$ is **topologically mixing** when for all nonempty open sets $U,V\subseteq X$ there is an integer $N$ such that

$$f^n(U)\cap V\ne\emptyset\qquad\text{for every }n\ge N .$$

2. A point $x\in X$ is a **periodic point** of $f$ when $f^n(x)=x$ for some $n\ge1$. The set of periodic points of $f$ is written $\operatorname{Per}(f)$. The periodic points are **dense** in $X$ when $\operatorname{Per}(f)$ is dense in $X$, that is ([[def-dense-top]]) when every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $\operatorname{Per}(f)$.

3. $f$ has **sensitive dependence on initial conditions** when there is a real number $\delta>0$ such that for every $x\in X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there are $y\in X$ and $n\ge1$ with

$$d(x,y)<\varepsilon\qquad\text{and}\qquad d\bigl(f^n(x),f^n(y)\bigr)\ge\delta .$$

Such a number $\delta$ is called a **sensitivity constant** for $f$.

Finally, say that $f$ is **chaotic in the stated sense** when $f$ is continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]), topologically mixing, has dense periodic points, and has sensitive dependence on initial conditions.

Let $(X, d_X)$ and $(Y, d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]), let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $a \in X$.

$f$ is **continuous at $a$** if for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that

$$d_X(x,a) < \delta \;\Longrightarrow\; d_Y\big(f(x), f(a)\big) < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for all } x \in X .$$

$f$ is **continuous** (globally, or on $X$) if it is continuous at every point of
$X$.

**The same condition in balls.** Since $d_X(x,a) < \delta$ says $x \in B_X(a,\delta)$
and $d_Y(f(x),f(a)) < \varepsilon$ says $f(x) \in B_Y(f(a),\varepsilon)$
([[def-metric-ball]]), continuity at $a$ reads: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there
is $\delta > 0$ with

$$f\big[B_X(a,\delta)\big] \subseteq B_Y\big(f(a), \varepsilon\big).$$

Both forms are used below and are the same statement written twice.

**Both metrics matter, and both are named.** Continuity is a property of the
triple $(d_X, d_Y, f)$, not of $f$ alone. When several metrics on the same
underlying sets are in play, as in [[def-equivalent-metrics]], the metrics are
always written out.

**Quantifier order.** The $\delta$ is allowed to depend on $\varepsilon$ **and on
the point $a$**. Requiring one $\delta$ to work at every point simultaneously is
a strictly stronger condition, uniform continuity; it is defined on a later page
of this library, and at this point in the reading order it is written out in full
where needed ([[def-equivalent-metrics]]).

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A **sequence in $X$** is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$, written $(x_k)$ with
$x_k := x(k)$. As everywhere in this library, $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]) and a sequence is indexed from $0$
([[def-sequence]]); an index range copied from a text that starts at $1$ must be
shifted before it is used here.

Let $(x_k)$ be a sequence in $X$ and $p \in X$. The function
$k \mapsto d(x_k, p)$ is a sequence of reals ([[def-sequence]]), and it is
nonnegative ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]), so $|d(x_k,p)| = d(x_k,p)$
([[def-abs-value]]). Define

$$x_k \longrightarrow p \text{ in } (X,d) \quad :\Longleftrightarrow \quad d(x_k,p) \longrightarrow 0 \text{ in } \mathbb{R},$$

the convergence on the right being that of [[def-real-limit]]. Unwound, this
says: for every **rational** $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$d(x_k, p) < \varepsilon$ for every $k \ge K$. We then call $p$ a **limit** of
$(x_k)$, and say $(x_k)$ **converges** in $(X,d)$ if it has a limit.

**Rational and real $\varepsilon$ agree here, as they do on the real line.**
[[def-real-limit]] tests convergence against rational $\varepsilon$ only, and its
own remark, restated for sequences in [[def-sequence]], records that nothing is
lost: below any real $\eta > 0$ lies a positive rational
([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), and the index belonging to that rational serves for
$\eta$. So a proof may establish convergence by producing an index for every
real $\varepsilon > 0$, and may use a convergence hypothesis at a real
$\varepsilon$ by first passing to a rational below it. Both moves are used on
this page and are always cited.

**Subsequences and subsequential limits.** A **subsequence** of $(x_k)$ is the
composite $x \circ n$ for a strictly increasing $n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$,
written $(x_{n_j})$, exactly as for sequences of reals ([[def-sequence]]); and
$p$ is a **subsequential limit** of $(x_k)$ in $(X,d)$ when some subsequence
converges to $p$, which is the metric-space form of [[def-subsequential-limit]].

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

derivations.claim: Choice of the threshold: put $\bar C:=\max(C_1,C_2)$ and let $\delta_0:=\min\bigl(\delta_1,\;1/(6\max(1,\bar C)),\;1/(\max(1,C)\max(1,\bar C))\bigr)>0$, so that for $0<\delta<\delta_0$ the number $\varepsilon:=\bar C\delta$ satisfies $\varepsilon\le1/6$ and $C\varepsilon\le1$.

Hypotheses of the perturbed horseshoe for $G_\delta$: by [F2] (with the identification of $G_\delta$ as the time-$P$ map in [F1]), for $0<\delta<\delta_0$ the maps $G_\delta$ and $H_\delta=S_w\circ G_\delta^{-1}\circ S_w$ are $C^\infty$, hence $C^2$, diffeomorphisms onto their images on a neighbourhood of $S$, and both satisfy each of the six componentwise closeness inequalities of [F3] on $S$ with the common constant $\varepsilon=\bar C\delta$; in particular $H_\delta$ is defined and $C^2$ on a neighbourhood of $S$ with the same inequalities. Thus the hypotheses of [F3] are met with $\varepsilon=\bar C\delta$.

Conclusions: applying [F3] to $G=G_\delta$ gives clauses 1-4 for the stroboscopic map: the coding homeomorphism $h_\delta$ onto a compact invariant set $\Lambda_\delta$ with $G_\delta\circ h_\delta=h_\delta\circ S_\pm$, chaotic behaviour of $G_\delta|_{\Lambda_\delta}$, the two hyperbolic fixed points of the constant codes, and transverse homoclinic points for all codes constant outside a finite set, in the sense of [F4]. Distinct codes give distinct points because $h_\delta$ is injective.

boundaries.reason: The code space and the coded set are nonempty images of the two-sign space, and the pulse has positive period P=pi/2+delta; no empty carrier is quantified.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 excludes delta=0 by the strict threshold delta_0>0 and step 2.1 applies the perturbed theorem with epsilon=C-delta; the degenerate case delta=0 is used only as the comparison map F in the approximation lemma.
Step 1.1 chooses one threshold and step 2.1 one application of the perturbed horseshoe theorem for each admissible delta; the sensitivity constant 2(sqrt(a)-3) is a single number.

Step 2.1 checks the two smallness conditions epsilon<=1/6 and C epsilon<=1 and step 3.1 records that distinct codes give distinct points; the constant codes give the degenerate periodic orbits of period one, hyperbolically.

Step 2.1 verifies the six componentwise closeness hypotheses on S including its boundary and step 3.1 handles codes constant outside finite sets, including the two constant codes; the time-P map is evaluated at the single period endpoint P.
The Statement and F3 explicitly assume Countable and Dependent Choice. These are inherited at step 3.1 from the supplier homeomorphism and compactness clauses, not erased during transfer.
Step 3.1 transfers the conjugacy G_delta circ h_delta=h_delta circ S_pm and the invariant-set conclusions of the perturbed theorem.
Step 3.1 also transfers injectivity of h_delta and the identification of the constant and finite-word codes, so the conclusions of clauses 1-4 hold exactly as stated.

citations.quote:
Fix $a\ge100$ and put

$$R:=\sqrt a+3,\qquad L:=\sqrt{\,a-2R\,}.$$

Let $X_{\pm}$ and $B_R$ be the two-sign shift space and the closed ball of bounded bilateral sequences of [[def-bilateral-symbol-and-bounded-sequence-space]], and for $s\in X_{\pm}$ define

$$T_s:B_R\longrightarrow \mathbb R^{\mathbb Z},\qquad (T_sx)_n:=s_n\sqrt{\,a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}\,}\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z).$$

Then:

1. $a-2R=(\sqrt a-1)^2-7\ge74$, so $L\ge\sqrt{74}>1$; moreover $a+2R<R^2$, hence $\sqrt{a+2R}<R$;
2. for every $s\in X_{\pm}$ and $x\in B_R$ the radicands $a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}$ lie in $[a-2R,a+2R]\subseteq(0,\infty)$, so $T_sx$ is a well-defined bounded sequence with $\|T_sx\|_\infty\le\sqrt{a+2R}<R$; in particular $T_s(B_R)\subseteq B_R$;
3. for all $x,y\in B_R$ and every $s\in X_{\pm}$,

$$\|T_sx-T_sy\|_\infty\le\frac1L\,\|x-y\|_\infty,\qquad \frac1L<1 ;$$

4. hence $T_s$ has, for each $s\in X_{\pm}$, exactly one fixed point $x(s)\in B_R$, and for every $n\in\mathbb Z$

$$\operatorname{sign}x_n(s)=s_n,\qquad |x_n(s)|\ge L,\qquad x_{n+1}(s)+x_{n-1}(s)=x_n(s)^2-a .$$

Write $\Sigma_{\pm}:=\{-1,+1\}$ and

$$X_{\pm}\ :=\ \Sigma_{\pm}^{\mathbb Z}\ =\ \{\,s\ :\ s \text{ is a function } \mathbb Z\to\Sigma_{\pm}\,\},$$

with the function-set convention of [[def-function-space]]; for $s\in X_{\pm}$ write $s_k:=s(k)$. The elements of $X_{\pm}$ are called **two-sign bilateral sequences**.

**Coding correspondence with the published two-symbol space.** Let

$$\varphi:X_{\pm}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z},\qquad \varphi(s)_k:=\frac{s_k+1}{2}\in\{0,1\},$$

and let $X_2:=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}$, $d_2$ and $\sigma_2$ be the set, the metric expression and the shift map of [[def-cm-bilateral-shift-space-and-cylinders]]. The formulas $\varphi(s)_k=(s_k+1)/2$ and $\varphi^{-1}(t)_k=2t_k-1$ define maps $X_{\pm}\to X_2$ and $X_2\to X_{\pm}$ that are inverse to each other, coordinate by coordinate.

**Metric expression on $X_{\pm}$.** Define

$$D_{\pm}(s,t):=d_2\bigl(\varphi(s),\varphi(t)\bigr)\qquad(s,t\in X_{\pm}).$$

Unwinding the series of [[def-cm-bilateral-shift-space-and-cylinders]] and using $|\varphi(s)_k-\varphi(t)_k|=\tfrac12|s_k-t_k|$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$ gives the explicit expression

$$D_{\pm}(s,t)=\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-(k+1)}\,|s_k-t_k|\;+\;\sum_{k\ge 1}2^{-(k+1)}\,|s_{-k}-t_{-k}| .$$

Both series converge by comparison with the geometric series $\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-k}=2$ ([[def-series]], [[thm-geometric-series]], [[def-integer-power]], [[def-abs-value]]), because $|s_k-t_k|\in\{0,2\}$ for every $k$; hence $D_{\pm}(s,t)$ is a well-defined nonnegative real number. Whether $D_{\pm}$ is a metric is **not** asserted here; it is proved in the companion lemma on this page, together with the statement that $\varphi$ is an isometry of $(X_{\pm},D_{\pm})$ onto $(X_2,d_2)$.

**The shift.** The **(bilateral) shift** of $X_{\pm}$ is

$$S_{\pm}:X_{\pm}\longrightarrow X_{\pm},\qquad S_{\pm}(s)_k:=s_{k+1}\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z,\ s\in X_{\pm}).$$

For $m\in\mathbb Z$ its iterate satisfies $S_{\pm}^{m}(s)_k=s_{k+m}$; in particular $S_{\pm}$ is a bijection with inverse $S_{\pm}^{-1}(s)_k=s_{k-1}$, and $S_{\pm}=\varphi^{-1}\circ\sigma_2\circ\varphi$.

**Bounded bilateral sequences.** A function $x:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$ is **bounded** when its range $\{x_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$ is a bounded subset of $\mathbb R$ ([[def-bounded-set]]). Write

$$\ell^{\infty}(\mathbb Z):=\{\,x:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R\ :\ x \text{ is bounded}\,\},\qquad \|x\|_{\infty}:=\sup\{\,|x_k|\ :\ k\in\mathbb Z\,\}.$$

The set $\{|x_k|:k\in\mathbb Z\}$ whose supremum is taken is nonempty and bounded above ([[def-bounded-set]]), so $\|x\|_\infty$ is a well-defined nonnegative real number ([[lem-sup-unique]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]). For $R>0$ put

$$B_R:=\{\,x\in\ell^{\infty}(\mathbb Z)\ :\ \|x\|_{\infty}\le R\,\}.$$

Thus $B_R$ is the closed ball of radius $R$ in the supremum norm, and $\|x\|_\infty\le R$ is by definition the statement that $|x_k|\le R$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$ ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-abs-value]]).

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-field]]).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of [[lem-power-laws]]: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors ([[lem-of-no-zero-divisors]]).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
([[lem-of-inverse-unique]]).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ ([[def-integers]]) is either
$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]],
[[def-int-operations]]). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$n$ for a unique natural $n$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]),
so $-m = n$ and $m = -n$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

derivations.claim: Endpoint inequality: $a+2R=100+26=126$ and $R^2=169$, so $a+2R<R^2$; by [L2] $\sqrt{126}<13=R$, which is the self-mapping inequality of [[lem-coded-quadratic-recurrence-is-a-contraction]]. Similarly $a-2R=100-26=74>1$, so $L=\sqrt{74}>1$ and $1/L<1$.

The fixed points: for $r_\pm=1\pm\sqrt{101}$ one has, using [L2], $$r_\pm^2=1\pm2\sqrt{101}+101=102\pm2\sqrt{101}=100+2(1\pm\sqrt{101})=100+2r_\pm .$$ Hence $(T_{\bar u}\tilde x)_n=u\sqrt{100+r_u+r_u}=u\sqrt{100+2r_u}=u\sqrt{r_u^2}=r_u$ by [L2] and $\operatorname{sign}r_u=u$, so the constant sequence $\tilde x_n=r_u$ is a fixed point of $T_{\bar u}$; by uniqueness it is $x(\bar u)$.

Bounds: $|r_\pm|\ge\sqrt{101}-1>9>\sqrt{74}=L$ and $|r_\pm|<12<13=R$, consistent with the general bounds of [L1]; the strict bounds $9>\sqrt{74}$ and $\sqrt{101}<11$ follow from $74<81$ and $101<121$.

boundaries.reason: The example evaluates the model at the fixed parameter a=100; there is no varying index set or family, so no empty-case value arises.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 computes a-2R=74>0 and step 1.2 uses the exact identity r_u^2=100+2r_u; the zero function is the starting point of the contraction but no vanishing radicand occurs.
Step 1.1 treats the single parameter a=100 and step 2.1 the two signs u=+-1 separately.

Step 2.1 verifies the constant sequences are fixed points by exact substitution and step 1.2 checks the strict bounds 74<81 and 126<169; the degenerate equality case a=100 is the borderline parameter itself.

Step 2.1 evaluates the identity r_u^2=100+2r_u at both signs and step 2.1 verifies the strict bounds |r_+-| between 9 and 12; the endpoints of the interval [l,R]=[7,13] are covered by the displayed comparisons.
The statement is verified by a finite sequence of exact algebraic identities and rational comparisons; no selection, limit or choice principle occurs.
Step 2.1 proves the constant sequence r_u is a fixed point of T_{bar u} by direct substitution.
Step 2.1 invokes the uniqueness clause of the contraction lemma to identify that fixed point with x(bar u), so the computed constants are exactly the coded values.

citations.quote:
**The quadratic family.** For $a\in\mathbb R$ let

$$F_a:\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad F_a(x,y):=(y,\,y^2-a-x),$$

with differential and inverse differential at $(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$

$$DF_a(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&2y\end{pmatrix},\qquad DF_a(x,y)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2x&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix};$$

the matrices act on column vectors of $\mathbb R^2$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). The inverse differential is displayed as the differential of $F_a^{-1}(x,y)=(x^2-a-y,x)$.

**Cones.** Fix $k\in(0,1)$. The **unstable cone** and **stable cone** of aperture $k$ are

$$C^u_k:=\{\,(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2\ :\ |u|\le k|v|\,\},\qquad C^s_k:=\{\,(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2\ :\ |v|\le k|u|\,\}$$

([[def-abs-value]]); both are closed subsets of $\mathbb R^2$, they are closed under multiplication by real scalars, and $C^u_k\cap C^s_k=\{0\}$, because a nonzero vector in the intersection would satisfy $|u|\le k|v|$ and $|v|\le k|u|$, hence $|u|\le k^2|u|<|u|$.

**Slopes.** A line through the origin not contained in the vertical axis is written uniquely as $\{(hv,v):v\in\mathbb R\}$ with the **slope parameter** $h=u/v$; here $|h|\le k$ characterises the lines contained in $C^u_k$. Similarly a line not contained in the horizontal axis is written uniquely as $\{(u,ru):u\in\mathbb R\}$ with the **slope parameter** $r=v/u$, and $|r|\le k$ characterises the lines contained in $C^s_k$.

For real numbers $x,y$ two maps on slope parameters are defined:

$$\Phi_y(h):=\frac{1}{2y-h}\quad(h\ne2y)\quad\text{(forward slope map)},\qquad \Psi_x(r):=\frac{1}{2x-r}\quad(r\ne2x)\quad\text{(backward slope map)}.$$

The intended reading is the graph-transform reading: $DF_a(x,y)$ carries the line $\{(hv,v)\}$ at $(x,y)$ to the line $\{(h'v,v)\}$ at $F_a(x,y)$ with $h'=\Phi_y(h)$, and $DF_a(x,y)^{-1}$ carries the line $\{(u,ru)\}$ at $(x,y)$ to the line $\{(u,r'u)\}$ at $F_a^{-1}(x,y)$ with $r'=\Psi_x(r)$. These two statements are assertions about the displayed matrices and are proved in the companion lemma on this page, not part of this definition.

**Invariant line fields on a sequence.** Let $s=(s_n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real bilateral sequence and let $z_n:=(s_{n-1},s_n)$. An **unstable line field along $s$** is a family $(L^u_n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ of lines through the origin of $\mathbb R^2$ such that $DF_a(z_n)$ maps $L^u_n$ onto $L^u_{n+1}$ for every $n$; a **stable line field along $s$** is a family $(L^s_n)$ with $DF_a(z_n)^{-1}$ mapping $L^s_{n+1}$ onto $L^s_n$ for every $n$. Existence and uniqueness of line fields with slopes in $[-k,k]$ for sequences with $|s_n|\ge L$ are proved in the companion lemma on this page.

**Stable and unstable sets, homoclinic and transverse homoclinic points.** Let $G:Z\to Z$ be a bijection of a metric space $(Z,d)$ ([[def-metric-space]]) with fixed point $\bar z$ (so $G(\bar z)=\bar z$). Put

$$W^s(\bar z):=\{\,z\in Z\ :\ G^n(z)\ \text{is defined for every }n\ge0\text{ and }G^n(z)\to\bar z\ \text{as }n\to\infty\,\},$$

$$W^u(\bar z):=\{\,z\in Z\ :\ G^{-n}(z)\ \text{is defined for every }n\ge0\text{ and }G^{-n}(z)\to\bar z\ \text{as }n\to\infty\,\},$$

where convergence is that of the metric $d$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]). The sets $W^s(\bar z)$ and $W^u(\bar z)$ are the **stable set** and the **unstable set** of $\bar z$. A **homoclinic point** of $\bar z$ is a point $z\in W^s(\bar z)\cap W^u(\bar z)$ with $z\ne\bar z$.

A homoclinic point $z$ is **transverse** when there are $\varepsilon>0$ and $C^1$ maps ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-derivative]])

$$\gamma_s,\gamma_u:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\longrightarrow Z$$

such that $\gamma_s(0)=\gamma_u(0)=z$, $\gamma_s\bigl((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\bigr)\subseteq W^s(\bar z)$, $\gamma_u\bigl((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\bigr)\subseteq W^u(\bar z)$, both $\gamma_s$ and $\gamma_u$ are injective on $(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ with $\gamma_s'(0)\ne0\ne\gamma_u'(0)$, and the tangent vectors $\gamma_s'(0)$ and $\gamma_u'(0)$ are linearly independent. The interval $(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ is that of [[def-interval]].

Let $a\in\mathbb R$, $k\in(0,1)$ and $L\ge2$. Let $s=(s_n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real bilateral sequence with $|s_n|\ge L$ for every $n$, put $z_n:=(s_{n-1},s_n)$, and let $C^u_k$, $C^s_k$, $\Phi_y$, $\Psi_x$, $DF_a$ and $F_a$ be as in [[def-stable-unstable-cones-and-line-slopes]]. Write

$$\lambda:=2L-k>1,\qquad \rho:=\lambda^{-2}<1,$$

and note that $1/\lambda<k$ because $k(2L-k)\ge k(4-k)>1$ for $L\ge2$ and $0<k<1$. Then:

1. **(cone invariance and expansion)** for every $n$: $DF_a(z_n)$ maps $C^u_k$ into itself, and every $(u,v)\in C^u_k$ satisfies

$$\max\bigl(|v|,\,|{-u}+2s_nv|\bigr)\ \ge\ \lambda\,\max(|u|,|v|);$$

and $DF_a(z_n)^{-1}$ maps $C^s_k$ into itself, with $\max(|2s_{n-1}u-v|,|u|)\ge\lambda\max(|u|,|v|)$ for every $(u,v)\in C^s_k$;
2. **(slope contractions)** for every real $y$ with $|y|\ge L$, the map $\Phi_y$ carries $[-k,k]$ into $[-1/\lambda,1/\lambda]\subseteq[-k,k]$ and satisfies $|\Phi_y(h)-\Phi_y(h')|\le\rho\,|h-h'|$ there; the same holds for $\Psi_x$ for every $|x|\ge L$;
3. **(unstable line field)** define $h^{(0)}_n:=0$ and $h^{(m+1)}_n:=\Phi_{s_{n-1}}\bigl(h^{(m)}_{n-1}\bigr)$ for $m\ge0$. Then $(h^{(m)}_n)_m$ converges for every $n$ to a limit $h_n\in[-k,k]$, uniformly in $n$, and

$$h_{n}=\frac{1}{2s_{n-1}-h_{n-1}}\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z);$$

furthermore $DF_a(z_n)$ maps the line $\{(h_nv,v):v\in\mathbb R\}$ onto the line $\{(h_{n+1}v,v)\}$ for every $n$, so the lines form the unique unstable line field along $s$ whose slopes all lie in $[-k,k]$;
4. **(stable line field)** similarly, $r^{(0)}_n:=0$ and $r^{(m+1)}_n:=\Psi_{s_n}\bigl(r^{(m)}_{n+1}\bigr)$ converge to limits $r_n\in[-k,k]$ with $r_n=1/(2s_n-r_{n+1})$, and $DF_a(z_n)^{-1}$ maps $\{(u,r_{n+1}u)\}$ onto $\{(u,r_nu)\}$; this is the unique stable line field along $s$ with slopes in $[-k,k]$.

Fix $a\ge100$ and put

$$R:=\sqrt a+3,\qquad L:=\sqrt{\,a-2R\,}.$$

Let $X_{\pm}$ and $B_R$ be the two-sign shift space and the closed ball of bounded bilateral sequences of [[def-bilateral-symbol-and-bounded-sequence-space]], and for $s\in X_{\pm}$ define

$$T_s:B_R\longrightarrow \mathbb R^{\mathbb Z},\qquad (T_sx)_n:=s_n\sqrt{\,a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}\,}\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z).$$

Then:

1. $a-2R=(\sqrt a-1)^2-7\ge74$, so $L\ge\sqrt{74}>1$; moreover $a+2R<R^2$, hence $\sqrt{a+2R}<R$;
2. for every $s\in X_{\pm}$ and $x\in B_R$ the radicands $a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}$ lie in $[a-2R,a+2R]\subseteq(0,\infty)$, so $T_sx$ is a well-defined bounded sequence with $\|T_sx\|_\infty\le\sqrt{a+2R}<R$; in particular $T_s(B_R)\subseteq B_R$;
3. for all $x,y\in B_R$ and every $s\in X_{\pm}$,

$$\|T_sx-T_sy\|_\infty\le\frac1L\,\|x-y\|_\infty,\qquad \frac1L<1 ;$$

4. hence $T_s$ has, for each $s\in X_{\pm}$, exactly one fixed point $x(s)\in B_R$, and for every $n\in\mathbb Z$

$$\operatorname{sign}x_n(s)=s_n,\qquad |x_n(s)|\ge L,\qquad x_{n+1}(s)+x_{n-1}(s)=x_n(s)^2-a .$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

derivations.claim: Fixed slope: the equation $h=1/(2r_+-h)$ is equivalent to $h^2-2r_+h+1=0$, whose roots are $r_+\pm\sqrt{r_+^2-1}$; the small root is $h=r_+-\sqrt{r_+^2-1}=1/(r_++\sqrt{r_+^2-1})$. Since $r_+>10$ and $\sqrt{r_+^2-1}>9$, one has $0<h<1/(10+9)<1/2$.

Cone constants: by [L3], $\lambda=2\sqrt{74}-\tfrac12>17-\tfrac12>1$; also $k(2L-k)=\tfrac12(2\sqrt{74}-\tfrac12)>\tfrac12\cdot16>1$, so the invariance and expansion hypotheses of [L1] hold with $\lambda=2\sqrt{74}-\tfrac12$. The induced bounds are $|\Phi_{r_+}(h)|\le\lambda^{-1}<1/2$ and $|\Phi_{r_+}(h)-\Phi_{r_+}(h')|\le\lambda^{-2}|h-h'|$ with $\lambda^{-2}<1/2$, in agreement with [L1].

boundaries.reason: The example fixes a=100 and one slope variable; no empty family or empty carrier is involved.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 solves the fixed-slope equation h=1/(2r_+-h) exactly and step 2.1 evaluates the slope map at h=0 as part of the interval estimate; h=0 is not the fixed slope but lies in the invariant interval.
Step 1.1 chooses the single small root of h^2-2r_+h+1=0 and step 2.1 the single aperture k=1/2 with lambda=2 sqrt(74)-1/2.
Step 1.1 verifies 0<h<1/(10+9)<1/2 with strict inequalities, and step 2.1 checks k(2L-k)>1 and lambda^{-2}<1/2; the discriminant r_+^2-1 is strictly positive because r_+>10.
Step 2.1 checks that the slope map carries the closed interval [-1/2,1/2] into [-lambda^{-1},lambda^{-1}] with lambda^{-1}<1/2, so both endpoints are mapped strictly inside.
The statement is a finite exact evaluation: every number is an algebraic expression in sqrt(101) and sqrt(74) with rational comparisons; no limit, simulation or choice is involved.
Step 1.1 derives the quadratic h^2-2r_+h+1=0 from the fixed-slope equation, so a fixed slope is a root of the quadratic.
Step 1.1 also verifies that the small root satisfies the fixed-slope equation, and step 2.1 that it lies in the invariant interval, so the two descriptions agree.

Fix $a\ge100$, let $R=\sqrt a+3$, $L=\sqrt{a-2R}$, let $x(s)$ and $h$ be the coded sequence and coding map of [[def-bilateral-symbol-and-bounded-sequence-space]], [[lem-coded-quadratic-recurrence-is-a-contraction]] and [[lem-symbol-locality-gives-coding-continuity]], and let $F(x,y)=(y,y^2-a-x)$. For $u\in\{-1,+1\}$ write $\bar u\in X_\pm$ for the constant code $\bar u_n:=u$, and put

$$r_u:=1+u\sqrt{a+1},$$

so that $r_+>0>r_-$, and write $W^s,W^u$ for the stable and unstable sets of [[def-stable-unstable-cones-and-line-slopes]]. Then:

1. $x_n(\bar u)=r_u$ for every $n$, and $r_u^2=a+2r_u$; consequently $h(\bar u)=(r_u,r_u)$ is a fixed point of $F$;
2. if $s\in X_\pm$ satisfies $s_n=u$ for all $|n|\ge N$ for some $N\ge0$, then

$$F^n\bigl(h(s)\bigr)\longrightarrow(r_u,r_u)\quad\text{as }n\to+\infty\quad\text{and as }n\to-\infty ;$$

3. if moreover $s$ is not the constant code $\bar u$, then $h(s)\ne(r_u,r_u)$, $F^n(h(s))\ne(r_u,r_u)$ for every $n\in\mathbb Z$, and $h(s)\in W^s(r_u,r_u)\cap W^u(r_u,r_u)$; hence $h(s)$ is a homoclinic point of the fixed point $(r_u,r_u)$;
4. distinct codes $s\ne t$ of the kind in clause 2 give distinct points $h(s)\ne h(t)$; in particular the finite-word deviations from the two constant codes produce infinitely many distinct homoclinic points.

Fix $a\ge100$ and let $R=\sqrt a+3$, $L=\sqrt{a-2R}$, $X_\pm$, $D_\pm$ and $B_R$ be as in [[def-bilateral-symbol-and-bounded-sequence-space]] and [[lem-coded-quadratic-recurrence-is-a-contraction]]. Define the **quadratic phase map**

$$F:\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad F(x,y):=(y,\;y^2-a-x),$$

and for each $s\in X_\pm$ let $x(s)$ be the unique fixed point of $T_s$ in $B_R$. Define the **coding map**

$$h:X_\pm\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad h(s):=\bigl(x_{-1}(s),\,x_0(s)\bigr).$$

Then:

1. $F$ is a bijection with $F^{-1}(x,y)=(x^2-a-y,\,x)$, and for every $s\in X_\pm$ and $n\in\mathbb Z$

$$F\bigl(x_{n-1}(s),x_n(s)\bigr)=\bigl(x_n(s),x_{n+1}(s)\bigr);$$

2. **(locality)** for all $m\ge0$, $n\in\mathbb Z$ and $s,t\in X_\pm$: if $s_j=t_j$ for all $j$ with $|j-n|\le m-1$, then $\bigl(T_s^m0\bigr)_n=\bigl(T_t^m0\bigr)_n$, where $T_s^m$ is the $m$-fold iterate and $0$ the zero sequence;
3. **(uniform error)** for all $m\ge0$ and $s\in X_\pm$,

$$\bigl\|T_s^m0-x(s)\bigr\|_\infty\le 2R\,L^{-m};$$

4. **(coding continuity)** if $s,t\in X_\pm$ agree at every coordinate $j$ with $|j|\le m$, then $|x_n(s)-x_n(t)|\le4R\,L^{-m}$ for $n\in\{-1,0\}$, and consequently

$$\bigl\|h(s)-h(t)\bigr\|_2\le4\sqrt2\,R\,L^{-m};$$

in particular $h$ is continuous at every $s\in X_\pm$ ([[def-metric-continuity]]) when $X_\pm$ carries $D_\pm$ and $\mathbb R^2$ the Euclidean metric;

5. **(injectivity)** $h$ is injective.

Fix $a\ge100$ and put

$$R:=\sqrt a+3,\qquad L:=\sqrt{\,a-2R\,}.$$

Let $X_{\pm}$ and $B_R$ be the two-sign shift space and the closed ball of bounded bilateral sequences of [[def-bilateral-symbol-and-bounded-sequence-space]], and for $s\in X_{\pm}$ define

$$T_s:B_R\longrightarrow \mathbb R^{\mathbb Z},\qquad (T_sx)_n:=s_n\sqrt{\,a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}\,}\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z).$$

Then:

1. $a-2R=(\sqrt a-1)^2-7\ge74$, so $L\ge\sqrt{74}>1$; moreover $a+2R<R^2$, hence $\sqrt{a+2R}<R$;
2. for every $s\in X_{\pm}$ and $x\in B_R$ the radicands $a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}$ lie in $[a-2R,a+2R]\subseteq(0,\infty)$, so $T_sx$ is a well-defined bounded sequence with $\|T_sx\|_\infty\le\sqrt{a+2R}<R$; in particular $T_s(B_R)\subseteq B_R$;
3. for all $x,y\in B_R$ and every $s\in X_{\pm}$,

$$\|T_sx-T_sy\|_\infty\le\frac1L\,\|x-y\|_\infty,\qquad \frac1L<1 ;$$

4. hence $T_s$ has, for each $s\in X_{\pm}$, exactly one fixed point $x(s)\in B_R$, and for every $n\in\mathbb Z$

$$\operatorname{sign}x_n(s)=s_n,\qquad |x_n(s)|\ge L,\qquad x_{n+1}(s)+x_{n-1}(s)=x_n(s)^2-a .$$

Write $\Sigma_{\pm}:=\{-1,+1\}$ and

$$X_{\pm}\ :=\ \Sigma_{\pm}^{\mathbb Z}\ =\ \{\,s\ :\ s \text{ is a function } \mathbb Z\to\Sigma_{\pm}\,\},$$

with the function-set convention of [[def-function-space]]; for $s\in X_{\pm}$ write $s_k:=s(k)$. The elements of $X_{\pm}$ are called **two-sign bilateral sequences**.

**Coding correspondence with the published two-symbol space.** Let

$$\varphi:X_{\pm}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z},\qquad \varphi(s)_k:=\frac{s_k+1}{2}\in\{0,1\},$$

and let $X_2:=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}$, $d_2$ and $\sigma_2$ be the set, the metric expression and the shift map of [[def-cm-bilateral-shift-space-and-cylinders]]. The formulas $\varphi(s)_k=(s_k+1)/2$ and $\varphi^{-1}(t)_k=2t_k-1$ define maps $X_{\pm}\to X_2$ and $X_2\to X_{\pm}$ that are inverse to each other, coordinate by coordinate.

**Metric expression on $X_{\pm}$.** Define

$$D_{\pm}(s,t):=d_2\bigl(\varphi(s),\varphi(t)\bigr)\qquad(s,t\in X_{\pm}).$$

Unwinding the series of [[def-cm-bilateral-shift-space-and-cylinders]] and using $|\varphi(s)_k-\varphi(t)_k|=\tfrac12|s_k-t_k|$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$ gives the explicit expression

$$D_{\pm}(s,t)=\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-(k+1)}\,|s_k-t_k|\;+\;\sum_{k\ge 1}2^{-(k+1)}\,|s_{-k}-t_{-k}| .$$

Both series converge by comparison with the geometric series $\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-k}=2$ ([[def-series]], [[thm-geometric-series]], [[def-integer-power]], [[def-abs-value]]), because $|s_k-t_k|\in\{0,2\}$ for every $k$; hence $D_{\pm}(s,t)$ is a well-defined nonnegative real number. Whether $D_{\pm}$ is a metric is **not** asserted here; it is proved in the companion lemma on this page, together with the statement that $\varphi$ is an isometry of $(X_{\pm},D_{\pm})$ onto $(X_2,d_2)$.

**The shift.** The **(bilateral) shift** of $X_{\pm}$ is

$$S_{\pm}:X_{\pm}\longrightarrow X_{\pm},\qquad S_{\pm}(s)_k:=s_{k+1}\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z,\ s\in X_{\pm}).$$

For $m\in\mathbb Z$ its iterate satisfies $S_{\pm}^{m}(s)_k=s_{k+m}$; in particular $S_{\pm}$ is a bijection with inverse $S_{\pm}^{-1}(s)_k=s_{k-1}$, and $S_{\pm}=\varphi^{-1}\circ\sigma_2\circ\varphi$.

**Bounded bilateral sequences.** A function $x:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$ is **bounded** when its range $\{x_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$ is a bounded subset of $\mathbb R$ ([[def-bounded-set]]). Write

$$\ell^{\infty}(\mathbb Z):=\{\,x:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R\ :\ x \text{ is bounded}\,\},\qquad \|x\|_{\infty}:=\sup\{\,|x_k|\ :\ k\in\mathbb Z\,\}.$$

The set $\{|x_k|:k\in\mathbb Z\}$ whose supremum is taken is nonempty and bounded above ([[def-bounded-set]]), so $\|x\|_\infty$ is a well-defined nonnegative real number ([[lem-sup-unique]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]). For $R>0$ put

$$B_R:=\{\,x\in\ell^{\infty}(\mathbb Z)\ :\ \|x\|_{\infty}\le R\,\}.$$

Thus $B_R$ is the closed ball of radius $R$ in the supremum norm, and $\|x\|_\infty\le R$ is by definition the statement that $|x_k|\le R$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$ ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-abs-value]]).

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

derivations.claim: Nonperiodicity of the code: for $m\ge1$, the coordinate $0$ of $S_\pm^ms$ equals $s_m=+1$, while $s_0=-1$; hence $S_\pm^ms\ne s$. Also $s\ne\bar{+1}$ because $s_0=-1$.
The point differs from the fixed point: by [L4], $x_0(s)<0<r_+$, so $h(s)\ne(r_+,r_+)$ directly; alternatively this follows from the injectivity and $s\ne\bar{+1}$ in [L1], [L2].
No return to the initial point: if $F^m(h(s))=h(s)$ for some $m\ge1$, then $h(S_\pm^ms)=h(s)$ by [L2], so $S_\pm^ms=s$ by injectivity, contradicting step 1.1.

Two-sided convergence: the code $s$ equals $\bar{+1}$ outside $\{0\}$, so [L1] applies with $u=+1$ and gives $F^n(h(s))\to(r_+,r_+)$ as $n\to\pm\infty$. Together with steps 2.1 and 2.2 this exhibits $h(s)$ as a nonperiodic homoclinic point of the fixed point $(r_+,r_+)$.

boundaries.evidence: The single-flip code differs from the constant code at the nonempty set {0}; the empty deviation set is the constant code handled separately in the parent lemma, and clause 4 of the example covers the general finite nonempty case.
Step 2.1 proves x_0(s)<0<r_+ using s_0=-1, so the coded point differs from the fixed point at the zero-th coordinate; no vanishing quantity is divided by.
Step 1.1 examines the single flipped coordinate 0 and its translates under the shift; the code is constant outside the one-point set {0}.
Step 3.1 excludes periodicity by comparing the unique flipped coordinate of S_pm^m s with that of s; the degenerate periodic case would force -m=0 and is impossible for m>=1.
the statement's applies the two-sided convergence of the finite-word lemma at both ends n->+infinity and n->-infinity.
Steps 1.1, 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1 combine the injectivity of the coding map and the explicit sign computation of [L4]; no limiting selection or choice principle is used.
Step 3.1 proves that F^m(h(s))=h(s) would force S_pm^m s=s by injectivity, contradicting step 1.1.
Step 1.1 shows S_pm^m s differs from s for every m>=1, so h(s) is not periodic; the two-sided convergence of step 3.1 exhibits it as a homoclinic point.

citations.quote:
The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

**The normalized pulse.** Fix once and for all a function

$$w\in C_c^\infty\bigl((0,1)\bigr),\qquad w\ge0,\qquad \int_0^1w(s)\,ds=1 .$$

Such a function exists: by [[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]] there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty((0,1))$ with $\chi\ge0$ and $\chi(1/2)>0$, and $w:=\chi/\int_0^1\chi$ has the stated properties, the integral being positive. All constructions below use only these properties of $w$ and are therefore independent of the particular choice.

**The periodic pulse.** Fix a real parameter $a\ge100$ and a smallness parameter $\delta>0$, and put $P:=\pi/2+\delta$. Define $\beta_\delta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ to be the $P$-periodic function whose restriction to $[0,P]$ is

$$\beta_\delta(t):=0\quad\Bigl(t\in\Bigl[0,\tfrac\pi2\Bigr]\Bigr),\qquad \beta_\delta(t):=\frac1\delta\,w\Bigl(\frac{t-\pi/2}{\delta}\Bigr)\quad\Bigl(t\in\Bigl[\tfrac\pi2,P\Bigr]\Bigr).$$

Both definitions are meaningful: for $t\in[\pi/2,P]$ the argument $(t-\pi/2)/\delta$ lies in $[0,1]$, and at the junction $t=\pi/2$ the second formula gives $\delta^{-1}w(0)=0$ because $w$ is supported in the open interval $(0,1)$; at $t=P$ it gives $\delta^{-1}w(1)=0$. Every derivative of $w$ vanishes at $0$ and $1$ (as $w$ is $C^\infty$ and compactly supported in $(0,1)$), so the $P$-periodic extension is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Moreover

$$\beta_\delta\ge0,\qquad \int_0^P\beta_\delta(t)\,dt=\int_0^1w(s)\,ds=1 .$$

**The Hamiltonian and its equations.** On canonical coordinates $(q,p)\in\mathbb R^2$ define

$$H_\delta:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad H_\delta(t,q,p):=\frac{p^2+q^2}{2}+\beta_\delta(t)\Bigl(aq-\frac{q^3}{3}\Bigr).$$

The associated first-order system is

$$q'=p,\qquad p'=-q+\beta_\delta(t)\,(q^2-a),$$

equivalently the second-order equation $q''=-q+\beta_\delta(t)(q^2-a)$; the right-hand side is $C^\infty$ in $(t,q,p)$, hence continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, so every initial condition has a unique maximal solution ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], [[def-maximal-ode-solution]], [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]). The system is $P$-periodic in $t$.

**Free rotation and pulse endpoint maps.** Over the first subinterval $[0,\pi/2]$ the pulse vanishes and the system is the free oscillator; define the **free rotation**

$$R_0:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2,\qquad R_0(q,p):=(p,-q),$$

which is the time-$\pi/2$ solution operator of $q'=p$, $p'=-q$: the map $t\mapsto(q_0\cos t+p_0\sin t,\,-q_0\sin t+p_0\cos t)$ solves the free system with the initial data $(q_0,p_0)$, and uniqueness of solutions identifies it with the solution operator.

For $s\in[0,1]$ the **rescaled pulse equation** is

$$q_s=\delta\,p,\qquad p_s=-\delta\,q+w(s)\,(q^2-a),$$

obtained from the second half of the period by the substitution $s=(t-\pi/2)/\delta$. For $(q,p)$ in its domain of existence, let the **pulse endpoint map** be

$$K_\delta(q,p):=\bigl(q(1),p(1)\bigr),$$

where $s\mapsto(q(s),p(s))$ is the unique solution of the rescaled equation with $(q,p)(0)=(q,p)$ ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]). The **stroboscopic map** of the periodic system,

$$G_\delta:=K_\delta\circ R_0,$$

is defined on the set of $(q,p)\in\mathbb R^2$ for which the solution of the $P$-periodic system exists up to time $P$; there it equals the stroboscopic map $\theta_P$ of [[def-cm-stroboscopic-map]]: the free rotation moves the initial point to time $\pi/2$, and the pulse endpoint map moves it from time $\pi/2$ to time $P$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

derivations.claim: Free rotation: by [L1] the displayed $(q,p)$ solves the free equations with the stated initial data, so by the uniqueness clause of [L4] it is the solution and the time-$\pi/2$ map is $(q_0,p_0)\mapsto(q_0\cos\tfrac\pi2+p_0\sin\tfrac\pi2,-q_0\sin\tfrac\pi2+p_0\cos\tfrac\pi2)=(p_0,-q_0)=R_0(q_0,p_0)$.

Kick: for $\delta=0$ the rescaled equation is $q_s=0$, $p_s=w(s)(q_0^2-a)$, whose solution with $q(0)=q_0$, $p(0)=p_0$ is the displayed one by [L1] and [L3]; evaluating at $s=1$ and using $\int_0^1w=1$ gives $K(q_0,p_0)=(q_0,p_0+q_0^2-a)$.
Composition: substituting $(q_0,p_0)\mapsto(p_0,-q_0)$ into $K$ and expanding gives $(K\circ R_0)(q_0,p_0)=(p_0,-q_0+p_0^2-a)=F(q_0,p_0)$, which is the displayed identity.

Pulse support and normalization: by [L2], $\beta_\delta$ vanishes outside $[\pi/2,P]$, is nonnegative there, and $$\int_0^P\beta_\delta(t)\,dt=\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi/2+\delta}\frac1\delta w\Bigl(\frac{t-\pi/2}{\delta}\Bigr)dt=\int_0^1w(s)\,ds=1.$$

Fix $a\ge100$ and put

$$R:=\sqrt a+3,\qquad l:=\sqrt a-3\ge7,\qquad S:=[-R-1,R+1]^2 .$$

Let $0<\varepsilon<1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open with $S\subseteq U$, and let $G=(A,B):U\to\mathbb R^2$ be a $C^2$ map satisfying the closeness hypotheses of [[lem-close-map-first-component-has-uniform-inverse]] on $S$ with constant $\varepsilon$; let $V:[-R,R]^2\to[-R-1,R+1]$ be its inverse branch. Define the **defect**

$$e(u,v,w):=-\bigl(V(v,w)-w\bigr)+2v\,\bigl(V(u,v)-v\bigr)+\bigl(V(u,v)-v\bigr)^2+B\bigl(u,V(u,v)\bigr)-\bigl(V(u,v)^2-a-u\bigr)$$

for $(u,v,w)\in[-R,R]^3$, and put

$$P_{u,w}(v):=v^2-a-u-w+e(u,v,w),\qquad (u,v,w)\in[-R,R]^3 .$$

Then:

1. $e$ is of class $C^1$ on $[-R,R]^3$, and there is a constant $C=C(a,R)$ such that $\|e\|_{C^1([-R,R]^3)}\le C\varepsilon$; in particular, with $\eta:=C\varepsilon$ assumed to satisfy $\eta\le1$, for all $(u,v,w)$

$$|e(u,v,w)|\le\eta,\qquad |\partial_ve(u,v,w)|\le\eta,\qquad |\partial_ue(u,v,w)|\le\eta,\qquad |\partial_we(u,v,w)|\le\eta ;$$

2. for every $(u,w)\in[-R,R]^2$ and each sign $s\in\{-1,+1\}$ the equation $P_{u,w}(v)=0$ has exactly one solution $v=M_s(u,w)$ with $s\,v\in[l,R]$, and this solution satisfies the margins

$$s\,M_s(u,w)-l\ge\tfrac34,\qquad R-s\,M_s(u,w)\ge\tfrac34 ;$$

moreover $M_s$ is of class $C^1$ on $[-R,R]^2$ with

$$\bigl|\partial_uM_s\bigr|\le d:=\frac{1+\eta}{2l-\eta},\qquad \bigl|\partial_wM_s\bigr|\le d ;$$

3. with $d$ as above and $\theta:=1/2$ one has, for every $a\ge100$ and $\eta\le1$,

$$d\le\frac2{13},\qquad 2d\le\frac4{13}<1,\qquad d\bigl(\theta+\theta^{-1}\bigr)\le\frac5{13}<1,\qquad \frac{d}{1-d\theta}\le\frac16<\frac23 .$$

4. **(orbit form of the root equation)** for all $(u,v,w)\in[-R,R]^3$,

$$P_{u,w}(v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B\bigl(u,V(u,v)\bigr)=V(v,w).$$

nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

derivations.claim: Endpoint signs: for $u,w\in[-13,13]$ the sum $u+w$ ranges over $[-26,26]$, so $v^2-100-u-w$ at $v=7$ is at most $49-100+26=-25<0$, and at $v=13$ is at least $169-100-26=43>0$.
Derivative bound and cone constants: substituting $l=7$, $\eta=1$ into $d=(1+\eta)/(2l-\eta)$ gives $d=2/13$, and the displayed inequalities follow from [L2].

Margins: with $\eta=1$ and $2R+\eta=27$, the root lower margin is at least $25/27>3/4$ and the upper margin at least $43/27>3/4$ (the example quotes the conservative bounds $24/27$ and $42/27$, which still exceed $3/4$); this is consistent with the general margins of [L1].

boundaries.reason: The example evaluates the perturbed recurrence at fixed a=100, l=7, R=13 and eta=1; no varying family or empty index set occurs.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 evaluates the unperturbed quadratic v^2-100-u-w at v=7 and v=13 for all u,w in [-13,13]; the endpoint values -25 and 43 are nonzero with strictly opposite signs, and no vanishing denominator occurs.
Step 2.1 substitutes the single parameter values l=7 and eta=1 into d=(1+eta)/(2l-eta) and obtains d=2/13.
the statement's uses the conservative margins 24/27 and 42/27, both strictly above 3/4, and step 2.1 verifies 2d=4/13<1 and d/(1-d/2)=1/6; the worst case eta=1 is exactly the evaluated borderline.

Step 1.1 evaluates the quadratic at the interval endpoints v=7 and v=13 for the extreme values u+w=-26 and u+w=26, giving the endpoint signs; the margins of step 2.1 measure the distance of the root from those endpoints.
The statement is checked by finite evaluations of polynomials and rational inequalities; no limit, selection or choice principle occurs.
Step 1.1 exhibits the strictly opposite signs of the quadratic at the two endpoints, which by the intermediate value theorem guarantees a root in [7,13].
